profile.reading:
Per Flexential's own individual facility page, this building (Flexential Salt Lake City - Fair Park) is located at 118 South 1000 West, Salt Lake City, UT 84104. The operator publishes a footprint of 22,539 square feet for this specific building; a critical-load UPS MW figure was not confirmed on the operator page and is not asserted here. Published certifications and compliance attestations include HITRUST CSF, SOC 1 Type II, SOC 2 Type II, SOC 3, SSAE 18. The facility page also highlights a base isolation seismic design intended to protect equipment during an earthquake, a notable engineering detail given the real seismic risk along Utah's Wasatch Front. This building is one of six Flexential locations serving the Salt Lake City market. Salt Lake City's data center sector is drawn in part by some of the lowest electricity and natural gas rates in the nation, historically around 5 to 6 cents per kilowatt-hour from a mix of natural gas and renewable generation, a cooling-efficient high-desert climate, and Utah's sales-and-use tax exemption for data center equipment purchases at facilities exceeding 150,000 square feet, retroactive to mid-2016, according to industry market analysis. Other major operators active in the broader Salt Lake City market include DataBank in Bluffdale, Aligned Data Centers in West Jordan, Novva Data Centers, QTS in Eagle Mountain, Meta, and Oracle, reflecting the area's shift from smaller retail colocation toward larger enterprise, HPC, and hyperscale capacity.

Flexential itself traces to the 1999 founding of ViaWest, which built out a Western US colocation footprint including Utah before merging with the Southeast-focused Peak 10 in 2017 and rebranding as Flexential in 2018; the company is now privately held with GI Partners as controlling sponsor. Utah's data center water use has drawn growing state scrutiny: a bill from Rep. Jill Koford, advanced unanimously by a legislative water panel in November 2025 for the 2026 session, would require data centers to report annual water consumption to the state under a $10,000-per-day fine for non-compliance, with individual figures kept anonymized publicly but available to state water officials. Reporting on the bill cited examples ranging from facilities using up to 5 million gallons a day, more than 12,000 times a typical household's usage, to the NSA's Bluffdale, Utah facility at about 23 million gallons annually, against low-water designs like Novva's reported 85,000 gallons; Koford said state water regulators had previously been left out of data-center water-use oversight, which had been handled mainly through city permitting.

reading.body:
The Flexential Salt Lake City - Fair Park facility publishes 22,539 square feet of technical space but no megawatt figure, making it impossible to estimate compute capacity or AI relevance from operator disclosures.

Certifications on the facility page—SOC 1 Type II, SOC 2 Type II, HITRUST CSF, and SSAE 18—indicate qualification for compliance-sensitive workloads in finance and healthcare rather than hyperscale training. These attestations define what can run there, not what does. The base isolation seismic design protects against earthquakes but does not indicate the power infrastructure or cooling capacity required for dense compute deployment.

Utah's 21 mapped data center facilities publish only 39 MW of capacity across three of them. This facility contributes zero to that figure. Without power disclosure from the operator, Fair Park remains unmeasurable as AI infrastructure. The pattern across the state suggests either small installations, private capacity held undisclosed, or both.
